Birth: An image that begins with a deletion

give me an image

Each section of this essay opens with a message the imagotchi shows at that stage of its image’s life. This first section explains what the device is, the question that led to it, and how I explored that question.

Fig. 1. Imagotchi (2026). ESP32, screen and touch sensor. Photograph by the author.The imagotchi is a small handheld device that holds a single photograph. A photograph from a personal album is sent over the device’s local network and compressed on arrival from 4,032 × 3,024 to 240 × 320 pixels, but the device accepts it only after the sender confirms that the copy on their phone has been erased (Fig. 1). From that point it holds the only instance of the image. Resolution is lost with time and with every edit or share, and the losses pause only when someone holds the device or answers its call. In a culture where almost nothing is deleted, this image’s life begins with a deletion.

The device grew out of an earlier question: whether disintegration could return some kind of originality to an endlessly circulating image by giving it a final destination. My iterations at that stage treated the image as a finite resource, with permanence in the source and transience in the rendering, and tried to give it a tangible body. I processed a single photograph through eight file formats, rebuilt its RAW data by hand across a hundred web pages, and divided its encoded fragments between NFC tags set into four clay pieces. Fig. 2. Cover of Alessandro Sbordoni, Beyond the Image: On Visual Culture in the Twenty-First Century (Set Margins’, 2025).Feedback from my tutor, Shaheer, changed the direction of this enquiry. The image had never stopped being physical, since it depends on material infrastructure for its storage, transmission and display. What my iterations were responding to is a condition I call obstructed physicality: the material existence of an image, the servers that store it, the cables that carry it and the screen that lights it, is hidden from the person looking, and with it any sense of what looking costs or asks of us. The more important question was what that obstruction does to the people who look. Alessandro Sbordoni’s Beyond the Image (2025) offered a way of answering it (Fig. 2). If “representation is a principle that no longer explains the image and its technology away”, then the value of an image lies in its reproducibility, and viewing itself is turned into data. Under these conditions the gaze is replaced by a stare “always-already centered on the device” (Sbordoni, 2025). The stare fragments attention. Images become interchangeable, each replaced by the next before it has been read, and the looking itself is logged. The gaze, as I use the term, is slower: an encounter with one image in which the viewer does part of the work of meaning.

This narrowed the enquiry to the question this essay pursues: what conditions can an image set for its own viewing, so that it is encountered with attention and not merely consumed? It is a question for graphic communication design because the discipline has largely accepted a division of labour. Designers decide what an image depicts, while platforms, formats and hardware set the terms on which it is seen: who receives it, at what quality, and what is extracted from the people looking. Physical computing gave me a way to work on those terms directly. Through a series of small prototypes, each reversing one quality of the stare and tested with peers, I explored what happens when an image asks something of the person looking at it, and the imagotchi grew out of these experiments.

I argue that the life of a digital image is sustained by the quality of attention it receives, more than by its resolution or its capacity to circulate. In tests of the earlier prototypes, images tended to hold attention best while they were incomplete, and the imagotchi carries that observation into a single device: its image stays whole only through care, and asks to be looked at as it loses detail. The rest of this text follows that image through its life, from what it inherits, through the works that shaped it, to its loss and what remains afterwards.

Origins: Where the image comes from

arrived at 240 × 320 (from 4,032 × 3,024)

As soon as the photo arrives, it loses most of its detail, shrunk to fit the device’s small screen. Like any digital image, it also carries a history it didn’t choose, of formats, networks and habits of looking. Part one of this section asks how we came to scroll past images instead of looking at them, which I call the stare. Part two looks at moments when technology could have developed differently, and at how they shaped the imagotchi.

Part one: How we learned to stare

From aura to performance: What reproduction did to the image?

My early iterations relied on Walter Benjamin’s account of mechanical reproduction, which locates the aura of an artwork in its unique presence in time and space and treats reproduction as its erosion (Benjamin, [1936] 1999). In my notes from the second week I wrote that images were simple while they stayed in the physical domain, and that technology had poisoned them with implications the average viewer cannot see. The questions I set myself followed from that: whether the “originality” of an image could be preserved in digital space, and how an image could be made real again.

Boris Groys’s In the Flow (2016) changed this view, because he argues that a digital image has no single original that could lose anything in the first place. The file itself is invisible, so the image exists only as a visualisation conjured each time the file is opened, much as a score exists as sound only when it is played, and aura moves from the original to each individual performance. Groys also writes that “in offline reality, the act of contemplation leaves no trace” (Groys, 2016), while online every performance of a file is dated and archived. My own files had shown me something similar. When I ran the photograph through the eight formats, I expected it to come out the Fig. 3. Format study, website prototype (2026). One photograph processed as DNG/RAW, TIFF, PNG and WebP, compared side by side. Screenshot by the author.same apart from its quality. Instead, every export left something behind: new metadata, a slightly altered look, a 28-megabyte RAW file reduced step by step to a palette JPEG (Fig. 3). If simply saving a file changed it, Groys’s claim that viewing it leaves a trace no longer seemed abstract. It also changed how I understood the study. I had set it up as a record of decline, from the best version of the photograph to the worst. What it actually showed was one file that no one ever sees, performed eight times, with each format deciding how much of the image a particular kind of user would receive.

Groys also helped me understand why ownership mattered so much in the project. People protect their images with watermarks, passwords and paywalls, trying to keep a private hold over files that circulate freely, and my clay pieces were my version of the same wish. The imagotchi continues it within limits. Its image is never uploaded to a platform, although the device does keep its own count of the care it receives.

When an image’s data could be held in the hand

The dot matrix in which the imagotchi renders its image has an older lineage, one in which image and data shared a material form. Manfred Mohr’s P-032 (Matrix Elements) (1970), a set of punched cards held by the V&A, carries both the instructions for a drawing and the record of them (Fig. 4). A program on cards had weight and an order that could be felt in the hand, and a dropped deck had to be sorted back card by card before anything could be drawn. Jean-François Blanchette (2011) shows that the record, the field and the file, the categories that still organise every stored photograph, come from punched-card data processing, and, drawing on Matthew Kirschenbaum (2008, cited in Blanchette, 2011), that file formats give data a formal materiality which limits what can be undone. Contemporary image software hides both. The dot rendering of the imagotchi brings some of it back onto the screen, presenting the image as a finite set of units that can be counted and lost.

Technology designed to disappear

Marshall McLuhan’s (1964) proposition that a medium restructures perception independently of its content implies that media act most forcefully where they are least perceived, and Mark Weiser (1991) turned this into a goal for computing: “the most profound technologies are those that disappear”. Olia Lialina’s “Turing Complete User” (2012) follows the cost of this to the person at the screen, who has been progressively written out of computing in favour of seamless, intuitive interfaces. She borrows Brenda Laurel’s description of computers that “became doors without doorknobs”. The smartphone takes this to the extreme. Held constantly, it delivers images to be scrolled past more than looked at, and an interface engineered to demand nothing of its user seems to me to produce images that demand little of their viewer. This is how the stare becomes habitual. I adopted Lialina’s metaphor as a working principle and tried to keep the doorknobs visible in the imagotchi. Its interactions are limited to a few physical buttons, and its resolution is kept low from the start, which restricts how far the image can be edited or decorated. Instead of hiding the image’s limits behind hyper-resolution, the device asks the person holding it to recognise them.

Fig. 4. Manfred Mohr, P-032 (Matrix Elements) (1970). Punched card. Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
Fig. 5. Illustration of divers inspecting a submerged ocean cable. From Lehdonvirta and Mikelsaar (2025).

The cloud is made of cables: the environmental cost of images

The internet has gone over and beyond its own boundaries. In “Too Much World: Is the Internet Dead?” (2013), Hito Steyerl describes a network that no longer stays on the screen. It persists offline, in her words, “as a mode of life, surveillance, production and organization”, and is better understood as an environment than as an interface. Yet the infrastructure that makes this possible, from cables on the seabed (Fig. 5) to data centres and satellites, is wrapped in a weightless vocabulary of clouds and streams that presents digital media as bodiless and almost magical. This, I think, is how the physicality of the image became obstructed in the first place: it was talked out of view.

Mindy Seu’s “The Internet Exists on Planet Earth” (2023) follows the cost of that language. Every transfer depends on energy, much of it still from fossil fuels, on extracted materials and on human labour. Viktor Mayer-Schönberger (2009) describes a digital culture of perfect remembering, in which keeping data has become cheaper than deleting it, but that cheapness is only financial: every image kept forever has to be stored and powered forever. Permacomputing, as practised by Hundred Rabbits (n.d.), offered me a different starting point, computing built around limits, repair and the resources actually available. This shaped the imagotchi’s functions. The build follows the same logic: like the cyberdecks people assemble from off-the-shelf parts, it is made from a few simple components (an ESP32 board, a small screen, a handful of buttons and a printed case), so its infrastructure stays modest, repairable and visible to whoever made it. The device sleeps by default and draws almost no power, holds one image instead of an archive, and erases that image at the end of its life. I had first thought of finitude as something poetic; after reading Seu, it became an ecological position as well.

Fig. 6. Yehwan Song, woldeu waideu (2022). Installation view.

Images made for machines: bias, class and resolution

Even after naming the stare, I could not fully explain why images had become so easy to pass over. Trevor Paglen’s “Invisible Images” (2016) gave me part of the answer: many images are no longer made for us at all. The function of the image, he argues, has shifted from representation and mediation to “activations, operations, and enforcement”, and most images are now made by machines for other machines. In the process, AI systems have taken human visual culture as a vast training set, one that sorts the people pictured in it by race, class and gender (Paglen, 2016).

The bias this produces is structural, because it is built into standards that are set before anyone looks. Batya Friedman and Helen Nissenbaum (1996) warn that once a biased system “becomes a standard in the field, the bias becomes pervasive”, and that such systems “offer no equivalent means for appeal”. Imaging has a long history of exactly this. Colour film was calibrated to white skin, so darker faces and dark objects reproduced as flat shadow (Pater, 2016), and the chemistry improved only when furniture and chocolate manufacturers complained that their products could not be photographed properly (Roth, 2009). Yehwan Song’s woldeu waideu (2022) shows a contemporary version: one video, compressed differently by each platform it passed through, leaves users of one supposedly shared web in different visual realities (Fig. 6).

My format study found the same logic at the level of resolution. Fig. 7. File information for the WebP version of the format-study photograph (2026). Screenshot by the author.It began with a question from my tutor in the second week, whether file types formed a hierarchy of their own, and laying out one photograph from a lossless RAW file down to a palette JPEG showed that they do (Fig. 7). Like film stock calibrated to one skin tone, or the platforms in Song’s work, each format is a standard decided before the image reaches anyone. The RAW file, heavy and readable only with specialist software, goes to professionals; the compressed JPEG goes to everyone else. Steyerl (2009) calls this a class hierarchy of images, in which ease belongs to whoever receives the rich version. Who receives which version of an image, and who is misread by the systems that consume it, are therefore questions of justice as well as of quality. This also gave my dot experiments a purpose I had not anticipated, which I return to in Care: if machines read sharp, complete images best, an image reduced to its dots can stay legible to a person while offering little to a dataset.

Read together, these sections locate obstructed physicality at several levels at once: in the file, whose material history has been forgotten; in the interface, designed to disappear; in the infrastructure, hidden behind weightless metaphors; and in the machine reader, for which the image is data before it is anything else. At each level the image asks less of the person looking at it and records more about them, and the stare is the habit that forms in between. None of these conditions was inevitable, and the second part of this section turns to how things could have gone differently.

Part two: How technology could have
gone differently

Webs that know their limits: Xanadu and the solar website

Fig. 8. Mockup of the Xanadu interface (1972). Reproduced in Ferenc (2015).The conditions behind the stare were designed, which means they could have been designed differently. Some alternatives have already been built or imagined. Ted Nelson’s Xanadu, developed from the 1960s, rejected the one-way hyperlink that can never be traced back to its source. Every link would be bi-directional, and instead of copying, a fragment would be transcluded, embedded as a live link to its original, so that a quotation could be followed back through all its earlier versions (Nelson, 1981) (Fig. 8). This felt close to how we relate to physical objects. We try to trace where something comes from, and even when we can’t, its material tells us something about its origin, which is part of how attachment forms. Fig. 9. The solar-powered server that runs Low-tech Magazine’s website. Photograph by Marie Verdeil. Reproduced in De Decker (2024).Low-tech Magazine’s solar-powered website reaches a similar restraint by another route (Fig. 9). It goes offline when the weather is bad, and its images are dithered into coarse dots to reduce the energy each page uses. I read both as attempts at bounding the boundless. The network was built on a promise of no limits: endless storage, constant availability, infinite copies. Xanadu puts a limit on copying, since every fragment stays tied to where it came from, and Low-tech Magazine puts a limit on energy, so the site exists only when the sun allows. In both, the limit is the starting point of the design.

I tried something similar, on a much smaller scale, with my clay pieces. Nelson’s rules for Xanadu read almost like rules for an object someone owns, and I tried Fig. 10. Clay pieces with embedded NFC tags, each holding part of an image’s data (2026). Photograph by the author.to apply some of them to an image. I kept it as text data instead of an image file and divided it between NFC tags set into four pieces of clay, each carrying a link to its part of the image rather than a copy of it, so that the image could be rendered only once someone had gathered them all (Fig. 10). The experience was too indirect for people to grasp straight away, but it was the first time an image in my work had to be held before it could be seen, and I wanted to carry this idea further in the iterations that followed.

Technology as a vessel: from Le Guin to the counter-conditions

Fig. 12. Finitude prototype (2026). Arduino, LCD1602 screen and real-time clock; the image disappears as its lifespan runs out. Photograph by the author.Fig. 11. The five qualities of the stare (2026). Diagram by the author.

In “The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction” ([1986] 1989), Ursula K. Le Guin retells human beginnings through the container instead of the weapon. Mammoth hunters dominate the cave paintings, yet most food was gathered, and the first cultural device was probably something to carry it in: “A leaf a gourd a shell a net a bag a sling a sack a bottle a pot a box a container. A holder. A recipient” (Le Guin, [1986] 1989). Her point is that the story of the spear has shaped what we think technology is for. She proposes judging a tool by what it holds rather than what it conquers, and telling life stories instead of heroic ones.

The technologies traced in this section have mostly been told as heroic stories of faster networks, sharper images and larger datasets. Le Guin offers a smaller measure: how well a tool keeps what it carries. A gathering tool is made with an intention of care, to hold something without damaging it, and the imagotchi follows the same idea. It re-situates the viewer as someone who looks after a single image, instead of someone who archives millions of them without looking at any.

Set side by side, the references in this section overlap in their diagnosis and in their refusal of the boundless. Steyerl, Seu and Mayer-Schönberger show the material cost of an internet that presents itself as weightless. Paglen, Friedman and Nissenbaum, and Song show who pays for vision built for machines and for Western defaults. Xanadu, Low-tech Magazine and permacomputing propose infrastructures that know their limits. Yet the conditions of viewing remain largely undesigned.

My counter-conditions were an attempt to work in that gap. I described the stare as a set of qualities (endless, habitual, quantified, device-centred and passive) (Fig. 11) and reversed each into a condition an image might set for its own viewing: finitude, friction, unmeasurability, situatedness and reciprocity. Each became a small prototype shown to peers (Fig. 12), designed as a carrier bag for an image and the attention given to it.

Care: Three works that shaped the device

you came.

If someone answers the device’s call and picks it up, the image appears in full and keeps its resolution. Three works shaped this design: Olia Lialina’s Summer, which exposes where an image is rendered; Hito Steyerl’s defence of the poor image, which made me see how circulation dulls our attention; and Trevor Paglen’s account of images made for machines, which shaped the device’s deliberately slow mechanics.

Olia Lialina, Summer (2013): life in infrastructure

Olia Lialina’s Summer (2013) looks at first like an ordinary GIF, a short loop of the artist swinging against a blue sky (Fig. 13). It is in fact a 21-frame animation in which every frame is hosted on a different server, and the browser is redirected from one address to the next to play it. How smoothly Lialina swings depends on the state of each connection, so the work is never seen the same way twice, and it stops altogether when a host goes down (Rhizome, 2013). Of her earlier work, Lialina said that with the “same files, same address, links” it had become “more like a documentation of itself” (Rhizome, 2013).

Fig. 14. MTAA, Simple Net Art Diagram (c. 1997). Reproduced in Rhizome (2013).What makes the piece interesting is how little it hides its own infrastructure. The URLs change visibly in the address bar, there is no preloader and no fallback, and when a server fails the animation simply breaks. Lialina lets the piece look poor so that it can show where it is being rendered, and on whose machines (Fig. 14). Fig. 15. Glitch experiments in Illustrator (2026). Image by the author.Rosa Menkman’s (2011) distinction between a glitch that has been domesticated into style and one that exposes the politics of the medium helps me see why my own first experiments fell short. In Illustrator I corrupted and distorted images until they broke apart (Fig. 15), but once I could choose and repeat the effect, it became a look I controlled rather than a crack in the system. My glitches decorated the surface of an image, while Summer’s breakdowns show the system underneath it.

The insight I carried from Summer was that exposing the medium can work against obstructed physicality and make infrastructure tangible. In the imagotchi I took this to the scale of the pixel. An image that looks whole is made of thousands of discrete units, and as the device loses resolution those units become visible one by one. The loss does two things: it lets the image’s structure be revealed, so the image is felt as a finite, grounded thing instead of a seamless surface. It also questions the hysteria over resolution that treats sharpness as the measure of an image’s worth.

Hito Steyerl, “In Defense of the Poor Image” (2009): life in circulation

Hito Steyerl opens her essay by calling the poor image an “illicit fifth-generation bastard of an original image” (Steyerl, 2009). When I first read it, the phrase made me question the condition of visual culture, but I don’t think I understood it fully until I had built a device in which an image is designed to die. Read again from there, her essay and my work answer the same question in opposite ways: where does the life of an image reside?

Steyerl’s answer is circulation. Images are ranked by resolution, and high resolution becomes a fetish, a marker of completeness and wealth. “Rich” images carry ease and privilege, while degraded copies give everyone else a blurry version of culture. Yet this loss is what makes the poor image democratic (Fig. 16). Compressed, it travels beyond its original carrier, finding new meanings as it moves, and works once locked away in archives are resurrected online. For Steyerl this makes it resistance and exploitation at once. An image lives in its afterlife; when it stops moving, it stops living. Her essay enacts this too: published freely on e-flux, it has circulated as countless PDFs and screenshots and become a poor image of itself.

Steyerl confirmed something Groys had already shown me: an image’s conditions of existence matter more than its relation to an original. Where I part from her is in what those conditions now do to us. Her essay was written in 2009, in a moment of abundance, and the speed she defends has since become the condition of the stare. Images are consumed as a flow instead of encountered one by one. If McLuhan is right that media reshape perception itself, this flow has made us less attuned to images, moving attention from interpretation towards quantity, so that we read visual culture in trends and aesthetics more than in single images. The leap from contemplation to distraction, which Steyerl treats with some ambivalence, seems to me the overlooked cost of circulation, and it is what has desensitised us.

The imagotchi was my attempt to find the opposite answer: a single copy that cannot be reuploaded, with its resolution shown as a number on the screen, which grows poorer when shared. Instead of granting the image an afterlife, I gave it a lifespan, hoping to make it more visible and more precious. I return later to whether this answer borrows from the hierarchy Steyerl describes.

Steyerl’s later writing shows where circulation leads now. In “Mean Images” (2023) she describes AI-generated images as the statistical median of pictures scraped into training datasets. Funnily enough, the circulation that once rescued images from the archive now delivers them to the dataset, which Trevor Paglen’s essay describes.

Trevor Paglen, “Invisible Images” (2016): life in elastic meaning

That images now feed training datasets is truly concerning, because it means their final destination has changed. They no longer end with a human presence; they are left to circulate and become the foundation for training sets. Paglen names this as the most critical change: most images are now made by machines for other machines, and human seeing has become the exception. Coming back to Groys, the image is conjured by a click, so what we see is only a rendering of data the computer read first. As images become quantifiable, the attention we give them can be measured and steered, and “smaller and smaller moments of human life are being transformed into capital” (Paglen, 2016). In this light, the stare looks like the human side of machine seeing: the quantification that empties our looking is what makes the image valuable to the system reading it.

Paglen’s own work shows that observation (Fig. 17): for Machine Readable Hito (2017) he photographed Hito Steyerl making hundreds of different expressions, and printed each picture with the output of facial-analysis software underneath, guessing her age, gender and emotion. Under one, the software decides she is 84.48 per cent female (Schwab, 2017). Laid out as a grid, the work shows each passing expression pinned to a single number.

What this system cannot reach is ambiguity. Human visual culture depends on the fact that “the relationship between meaning and representation is elastic”, and for Paglen that elasticity “simply ceases to exist” in machine seeing (Paglen, 2016). A person can hold several readings of an image at once, guess and fill in what is missing. How, then, can we make images that keep their meaning open?

Paglen’s answer is to create “deliberate inefficiencies”: processes made slower, harder or less legible than they need to be, so that they fall outside what a system can measure and turn into data. He describes them as “safe houses” in the digital sphere, spaces kept apart from market and political predation, and locates freedom and political self-representation in this kind of inefficiency (Paglen, 2016). Fig. 18. Kensuke Koike, Emergency Call (2013). Switched vintage photograph, 13.5 × 8.5 cm. From the series Single Image Processing.Luna Maurer and Roel Wouters’s manifesto Designing Friction (2023) makes a similar call from inside design, for the slowness and clumsiness that seamless products were built to remove. For an image, an inefficiency is anything that makes it ask for effort before it gives itself up: a gap to fill, a delay, a missing part. That effort keeps its meaning with the person looking.

Fig. 19. Circular-shift experiment (2026). p5.js. Image by the author.Fig. 20. Dot reconstruction experiment (2026). p5.js. Image by the author.I tested this first by creating a deliberate gap. I was deeply inspired by Kensuke Koike’s collages, which cut and rearrange archival photographs so that you decipher the original while reading the changes made to it (Fig. 18). Using similar tactics, I rebuilt photographs in p5.js from their own dots and blocks (Figs. 19–20). Through these iterations I realised how important the space between the image and the viewer is: the power of interpretation. The more effort an image takes to decipher, the more you cherish its leftover pieces.

Paglen’s idea also shaped how the imagotchi works. From the moment it arrives, its image is already poor, reduced to 240 × 320 and drawn in dots, so the viewer has to work for the gaze, piecing the picture together and remembering what the photograph once showed. The dotted image sits in exactly the gap Paglen describes, where meaning stays elastic. The device then adds a second kind of effort. Its image resolves only when someone holds it and stays with it, which makes physical presence part of looking: it cannot be consumed from a distance or in passing, only in the hand. Where the dot experiments asked for imaginative effort, the imagotchi asks for physical and temporal effort too, a symbiotic relationship in which the image depends on the person and the encounter gives something back.

Neglect: When the image loses its detail

I called. you didn’t come.

When its calls go unanswered, the image begins to lose its detail one pixel at a time, until faces and edges dissolve into blocks of colour. Here the device is tested against Steyerl. She argues that sharp, high-resolution images belong to the privileged, and by measuring the image’s health in sharpness, the imagotchi seems to share that view. What I saw when classmates tried my earlier prototypes suggested otherwise: the incomplete images were the ones that held them, as if the gap itself asked them to pay attention.

If its calls go unanswered, the image loses pixels, and the counter on its screen records each loss (Fig. 21). This is also where the device comes closest to the hierarchy Steyerl criticises. Sharpness becomes the measure of the image’s health, and a photograph that cannot be shared at full quality looks like scarcity, the rich image in a new form. In trying to rescue the image from circulation, I appeared to have adopted the hierarchy circulation was meant to undo. I don’t think the image is valuable because it is rare. Its value lies in reliance: it cannot keep its resolution without being held, and the person cannot see it fully without holding it. The counter records that relationship, how well the image has been looked after, rather than what the image is worth.

Fig. 21. The imagotchi’s image losing resolution, from 240 × 320 to a single pixel (2026). Image by the author.

What I observed in prototyping and testing supports this. When I showed the counter-condition prototypes to peers, the incomplete images were the ones that kept people looking. Katka asked whether the image needed to be assembled at all, since the missing detail was what held her interest. Another classmate noted that it was never the same image twice: it became important because the person looking had become the variable. Dan Hays describes the same effect in his paintings of low-resolution webcam images, which “invite imaginative projection, for the visual cortex to work to fill in the blanks” (Hays, n.d.). Family archive photographs work in a similar way. As they fade, we hold on to them more closely and try to recall what they once showed. This is the elasticity Paglen says machines cannot read. The imagotchi’s image calls for attention at the moment it is losing detail, and the earlier tests suggest this is when an image is looked at most closely. Losing resolution takes something from the image, but it also gives something back, which brings my work closer to Steyerl than I expected.

Where I still part from Steyerl is in how she values the poor image’s movement. She writes that poor images’ “lack of resolution attests to their appropriation and displacement” (Steyerl, 2009), and her essay defends images that lose matter and gain speed as they travel. Read today, that position sits close to the illusion of weightlessness I traced earlier, an internet imagined as able to hold everything forever. I don’t believe an image should be displaced, left in the network with no home of its own, and the romantic picture of the wandering poor image no longer feels plausible to me. In a culture where nothing is deleted, the imagotchi’s image begins with a deletion, becomes poor in one place, with one person, and ends where it was kept. Its life lay in the attention it received, and if that is true, there is little reason left to measure its health in resolution at all.

Afterlife: What remains, and what comes next

Fig. 22. Imagotchi (2026) at the end of its image’s life, showing a single colour. Photograph by the author.I am one colour now.

At the end of its life, the image becomes a single colour, the average of everything it once showed, and then it is erased for good. The device stays and asks for a new photograph. This last section draws together what the image’s life suggests for how designers work with images, and where the project could go next.

The imagotchi ends where it began, with a deletion. For its last day the image is a single field of colour (Fig. 22), the average of everything it once showed, and then it is erased. Nothing is kept from it, yet its end is still marked: the screen shows a small RIP, so the loss is noticed instead of passing in silence, and the attention the image received is acknowledged one last time. In a culture of perfect remembering, this may be the most unusual thing the device does: it lets an image finish.

Following that image through its life confirms the argument I began with. An image is kept alive by the attention it receives, more than by its resolution or by how far it travels. The conditions that shape that attention are as open to design as anything an image depicts: how long it lasts, what it asks of the person holding it, where it can be seen, and what is recorded about the looking. At present they are set by default, and mostly for machines.

What the work untangles is care from ownership. The image in the imagotchi matters because someone keeps returning to it, not because they possess it. Yet withdrawing a private image from circulation may protect it from extraction while producing the rich image in a new form, singular and kept for one person. This leaves me with a sharper question to carry forward: in a culture of hyperconnectivity and constant production, can an image move the viewer from stare to gaze while embracing, rather than resisting, its condition as a poor image, and can that care be shared without relying on circulation?
